title: "We Don't Hire Friends"
author: M. Perrone
summary: M. Perrone argues against the widespread conventional wisdom that business and friendship must be kept separate, framing this separation as both a symptom and a cause of the crisis of male community in contemporary life. The inciting moment is a social gathering where one couple declines to hire a competent friend, citing the standard objections: risk of awkwardness, potential for disagreement, danger to the friendship. Perrone identifies this as structurally parallel to the romantic 'I care about you too much to ruin our friendship' — both are fundamentally withholdings of personal commitment that preserve a comfortable but shallow status quo. The deeper argument concerns men specifically: modern life has systematically removed the practical contexts in which men once developed deep trust, loyalty, and the felt sense of having each other's backs — hunting, barn-raising, collective defence — leaving only passive consumption-oriented togetherness where nothing of real consequence is at stake. Doing business with competent friends, Perrone contends, forces development of relational skills the anonymous market deliberately eliminates: confrontation, forgiveness, honest expectation-setting, accountability, and genuine communication. The article concludes that cautious and judicious embrace of social liability is the structural difference between the atomised individual and the man embedded in a village of others who genuinely have his back.
points: The refusal to do business with friends mirrors the romantic 'I care about you too much to ruin our friendship' — both are withholdings of personal commitment that preserve shallow status quo rather than risking the deeper stakes that produce genuine relationship.

Modern life has eliminated the structural contexts in which men once developed trust, loyalty, and mutual obligation through shared high-stakes work; consumer entertainment (watching games, splitting pizza tabs) keeps nothing real at stake and therefore cannot produce the felt security of genuine mutual backing.

Doing business with competent friends forces acquisition of relational skills — confrontation, forgiveness, explicit expectation-setting, accountability — that purely anonymous market transactions are specifically designed to make unnecessary, and which cannot be developed without practice in real-stakes contexts.

The arms-length market economy efficiently processes transactions but cannot produce the felt experience of having someone's back; its anonymity protects from betrayal but simultaneously prevents the loyalty and trust that come only from shared stakes and real risk.

Men need contexts where something of genuine consequence is at stake in their relationships; without this, even a large social circle provides company without the felt security of mutual obligation that distinguishes a village from a collection of acquaintances.
quotes: Fundamentally, it's a withholding of personal commitment; a stated desire to keep the safe and predictable status quo; or perhaps just a nice way to avoid uncomfortable and awkward conversations.

Everyone that I count on and everyone that I pay needs to be held at arms length, so that I can sue them, drop them, write a one star review, or not feel betrayed by them in case something goes wrong.

'We don't do business with or hire friends.' This is fundamentally the same statement as the romantically lethal: 'I care about you too much to ruin our friendship'; a withholding of personal commitment; a stated desire to keep the safe and predictable status quo.

One of the greatest compliments a man can give to another man is saying some guy 'has my back' or a similar expression of that feeling of duty, shared obligation and loyalty. A man with thousands of other men to talk with and understand him may still feel very lonely. But a man with just a handful of other guys who 'have his back' is never alone. And that, more than a shoulder to cry on, can change his life.

Modern life has already removed so many contexts where men can have each other's backs. We cannot hunt for necessities together, we cannot raise barns together, we cannot patrol and protect our tribe together. It's difficult to work daily together on almost anything.

No, something, somewhere along the line has to count, someone needs to have our back, which means there has to be risk. We need to feel the loyalty, the trust, the respect, and the dignity that can't be provided by arms-length, impersonal transactions with corporations.
The careful and judicious embrace of some social liability is the difference between the lonely, radical individual and the man who has a village full of other guys who truly have his back.
